html:
The alphabet used to write Greek since the late 800s or early 700s BCE. Greeks took it from the Phoenician alphabet, probably through trade, and kept the order and many of the names: aleph and beth became alpha and beta.

Phoenician writing had signs only for consonants. The Greeks used letters for sounds their language lacked to write vowels instead, which made theirs the first full alphabet with both. Early Greek came in several local versions, written right to left or in alternating lines before left to right won out. Athens adopted the Ionic version in 403 BCE, and it became the standard.

The alphabet spread reading and writing among Greeks, and with it the written poems of Homer, history and philosophy. Its offspring include:

  • the alphabet of the Etruscans, and from it the Latin alphabet;
  • Coptic in Egypt, and Gothic;
  • the Cyrillic script, made in Bulgaria in the 890s CE.

Greek letters are still used in mathematics and science.
